title: A Good Marriage and the End of Crime
text:
In the 1940s, the criminologists Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck at Harvard began following 500 boys from Boston who had been sent to reform schools for delinquency, along with 500 boys from similar neighborhoods who had not. They tracked the delinquent group into their thirties. Decades later, John Laub and Robert Sampson found the Gluecks' records in boxes in the basement of the Harvard Law School library and set out to analyze them with modern methods.

In a 1998 study with the statistician Daniel Nagin, they looked at how the former delinquents' offending changed over adulthood. Some men kept committing crimes; others gradually stopped. The researchers asked what life events went along with stopping.

Marriage stood out, but only a certain kind. It was not the wedding that mattered, but forming a good, cohesive marriage: one in which the man was attached to his wife and the bond was strong. Men who formed such marriages tended to reduce their offending, and the effect built up gradually over the years, as the relationship deepened and daily life changed. Weak marriages showed no such benefit.

Laub and Sampson argued that strong bonds give men something to lose, reshape their routines and connect them with new friends and family.
lesson: People can change at any age, especially when they have a strong bond to protect. A committed relationship can reshape a life over time.
people: John Laub, Daniel Nagin, Robert Sampson
source: Laub, J. H., Nagin, D. S., and Sampson, R. J. (1998). Trajectories of change in criminal offending: Good marriages and the desistance process. American Sociological Review, 63(2), 225-238.
caveat: The data were observational, so men who were already changing may have been more likely to form good marriages.
